Three years ago, I thought remote work meant working from anywhere. Now I know it means working from intention.

The biggest shift wasn't the commute disappearing. It was realizing that visibility no longer comes from being seen at your desk — it comes from the clarity of your communication.

A few things that have made the difference for our team:

• Writing things down, even when it feels redundant
• Default to async, but protect time for real connection
• Trusting outcomes over hours

Remote work isn't a perk. It's a skill. And like any skill, it gets better with practice.

What's one habit that's made remote work better for you?

If you've ever stared at a blank code editor wondering where to even begin, you're not alone. Learning to code can feel overwhelming at first — there are countless languages, frameworks, and tutorials all competing for your attention. The good news? You don't need to learn everything at once. In this post, I'll walk you through a practical, step-by-step approach to getting started, from choosing your first language to building a project you're genuinely proud of.

With precise temperature control from 40°C to 100°C, you can brew everything from delicate green teas to bold French press coffee exactly the way it's meant to be. The keep-warm function holds your chosen temperature for up to two hours, and the companion app lets you start boiling before you've even left bed. Tucked away on a quiet side street, Osteria Lume is the kind of place you want to keep to yourself. The space is small and warmly lit, with just a dozen tables and an open kitchen that fills the room with the scent of garlic and wood smoke. We started with the burrata, which was creamy and perfectly balanced by a drizzle of good olive oil and a scattering of charred tomatoes. The standout, though, was the cacio e pepe — silky, peppery, and deceptively simple. Service was attentive without being intrusive, and the wine list offers thoughtful options at reasonable prices. It's not the cheapest dinner in town, but it's easily one of the most memorable.

Project Hail Mary is a rare kind of science fiction novel: one that's genuinely fun to read while still taking its science seriously. Andy Weir builds the story around a single, compelling mystery — a man wakes up alone on a spacecraft with no memory of how he got there — and then layers in flashbacks that gradually reveal the stakes. What elevates the book, though, is the unexpected friendship at its heart, which gives the problem-solving a surprising emotional weight. Some readers may find the protagonist's constant cheerfulness a bit much, but by the final chapters, it's hard not to be completely invested.

Honestly, the thing that helped me most with sleep wasn't any supplement or gadget — it was being really consistent with my wake-up time, even on weekends. It felt brutal for the first week or two, but after that my body just started getting tired at a reasonable hour on its own. The other big one was cutting caffeine after noon. I didn't think it was affecting me, but it definitely was. Worth trying both for a couple of weeks before spending money on anything else.
Hot take: most productivity problems aren't time management problems. They're clarity problems. When you know exactly what the next step is, the motivation usually follows.

I've been running a small bakery for five years. Here are the lessons nobody told me when I started: 🧵

1/ Your best customers aren't the ones who spend the most. They're the ones who come back every week and bring their friends.

2/ Waste is the silent killer of margins. Track it obsessively.

3/ Your staff will care about the business exactly as much as they feel cared for.

4/ Consistency beats creativity. People come back for the croissant they loved last time.

Bergen is often called the gateway to the fjords, and for good reason — but it's well worth slowing down and spending a few days in the city itself. Start at Bryggen, the colorful row of historic wooden buildings along the harbor, then take the Fløibanen funicular up Mount Fløyen for sweeping views over the city and surrounding mountains. From there, several well-marked trails lead deeper into the forest. Be prepared for rain: Bergen is one of the wettest cities in Europe, so a good waterproof jacket is essential no matter the season.

The city council voted on Tuesday to expand the bike lane network by 40 kilometers over the next three years, a plan supporters say will make cycling safer and reduce traffic congestion. The proposal passed 9–4 after a lengthy debate, with opponents raising concerns about the loss of parking spaces in several commercial districts. Construction is expected to begin next spring, starting with routes connecting the university to the city center. Officials estimate the total cost at €62 million, with roughly half covered by national transportation grants.

You don't need to have it all figured out to take the next step.

Most of the people you admire started before they felt ready. They made mistakes in public, learned as they went, and kept showing up when it would have been easier to quit.

Progress rarely looks impressive up close. It looks like small, unremarkable days stacked on top of each other.

So take the next step. Just one. The rest will come.

Great question — this trips up a lot of people when they first start with Python. The short answer is that `is` checks whether two variables point to the exact same object in memory, while `==` checks whether their values are equal. So two different lists containing the same elements will be `==` but not `is`. In practice, you should almost always use `==` for comparing values. The main exception is checking for `None`, where `is None` is the recommended style. Hope that helps clear it up!

Attention has quietly become one of the most contested resources of modern life. Every app, platform, and notification is engineered to capture a little more of it, often at the expense of the deeper, slower forms of focus that meaningful work and relationships require. What makes this shift so difficult to resist is that it rarely feels like a loss in the moment; each individual distraction seems small and harmless. Yet over time, these fragments add up to a fundamentally different way of experiencing the world — one in which sustained thought becomes the exception rather than the rule.

It's been a busy few weeks here, and I have a lot to share. Autumn has officially arrived in Berlin — the mornings are crisp, the light is golden, and I've finally started wearing a proper jacket again. This issue is a bit longer than usual, because I wanted to dig into something that's been on my mind lately: why so many of us feel busy all the time, yet struggle to point to what we've actually accomplished. Grab a coffee, and let's get into it.

Moving to a new city at thirty felt, at first, like starting over in the worst possible way. I didn't know anyone, I couldn't find a decent grocery store, and every small task seemed to take twice as long as it should. But somewhere around the third month, something shifted. I started recognizing faces at the café on the corner. I found a running route I loved. And I realized that the discomfort of being new had forced me to become more open, more curious, and more willing to ask for help than I had been in years.

Growing tomatoes at home is one of the most rewarding gardening projects you can take on, even if you only have a small balcony. With the right variety, a sunny spot, and a bit of consistent care, you can enjoy fresh, flavorful tomatoes all summer long. This guide covers everything you need to get started, from choosing seeds or seedlings to watering, feeding, and harvesting — plus a few common problems to watch out for along the way.

When a reclusive lighthouse keeper on a remote Scottish island discovers a shipwrecked stranger with no memory of her past, his carefully ordered life begins to unravel. As a winter storm cuts the island off from the mainland, the two form an uneasy bond — until fragments of the woman's identity start to surface, raising questions neither of them is prepared to answer. Atmospheric and quietly suspenseful, The Last Light is a meditation on isolation, trust, and the stories we tell ourselves to survive.

Something I keep coming back to: the most useful thing you can do for your future self is write down what you were thinking when you made a decision. Not just what you decided — why. Six months later, the context is gone, and you're left second-guessing choices that probably made perfect sense at the time.

We hired six engineers this year, and the most important thing I learned had nothing to do with technical interviews.

The best signal wasn't how quickly someone solved a problem. It was how they talked about the parts they didn't know.

The candidates who said "I'm not sure, but here's how I'd find out" consistently turned out to be the strongest teammates. They asked better questions, learned faster, and made everyone around them better.

Confidence is easy to perform. Curiosity is much harder to fake.

Curious how others think about this — what's the most reliable signal you've found in hiring?

Most personal finance advice starts with a budget. This post doesn't. Instead, I want to start with a question that I think matters more: what do you actually want your money to do for you? Once you have a clear answer, the practical decisions — how much to save, where to invest, what to cut back on — become much easier to make. Let's walk through how to figure that out, and how to build a simple system around it.

The Trailhead 28L backpack is built for day hikes that turn into longer adventures. A lightweight aluminum frame and ventilated back panel keep you comfortable on steep climbs, while the water-resistant fabric protects your gear when the weather turns. Inside, you'll find a dedicated hydration sleeve, an organized top pocket for small essentials, and plenty of room for layers and snacks. Adjustable hip and sternum straps ensure a secure fit, whether you're heading up a local trail or exploring the fjords.

Kaffeehaus Morgen has quickly become my go-to spot for a slow weekend breakfast. The menu is short but carefully chosen: think soft scrambled eggs on sourdough, house-made granola with seasonal fruit, and a surprisingly excellent cardamom bun. The coffee is roasted locally and made with real care, and the baristas are happy to talk you through their current beans. It can get busy after ten, so arrive early if you want one of the window seats.

As someone who switched careers into software at 34, I'd say don't let your age discourage you at all. Your previous experience is actually an advantage — you know how workplaces function, how to communicate with non-technical people, and how to manage your time. The hardest part for me was getting the first job, so I'd focus on building two or three solid projects that solve real problems rather than doing dozens of tutorials. And network more than feels comfortable. Most of my interviews came through people I'd met at local meetups.

The Remains of the Day is a quiet novel that lingers long after you finish it. Kazuo Ishiguro tells the story entirely through the voice of Stevens, an aging English butler reflecting on decades of loyal service, and much of the book's power comes from what Stevens refuses — or is unable — to say. Beneath his formal, restrained narration lies a profound sense of regret about love, loyalty, and a life lived in service of someone else's ideals. It's a subtle, beautifully controlled book that rewards patient reading.

A new study published this week suggests that short daily walks may significantly reduce the risk of heart disease, even for people who don't meet standard exercise guidelines. Researchers followed more than 15,000 adults over eight years and found that those who walked at least 20 minutes a day had a 21% lower risk of cardiovascular events compared with those who walked less. The authors caution that the study was observational and cannot prove cause and effect, but they say the findings add to growing evidence that modest activity has meaningful health benefits.

Rest is not a reward for finishing your work. It's part of the work.

We've been taught to push through, to earn our breaks, to treat exhaustion as proof of commitment. But the people who do their best work over the long run are the ones who know when to stop.

Take the walk. Close the laptop. Sleep in once in a while.

You'll come back sharper — and you'll last longer.

The key thing to understand about sourdough starters is that they're living cultures, so consistency matters more than precision. If yours isn't rising, the most common culprits are temperature and feeding schedule. Try keeping it somewhere around 24–26°C and feeding it at the same times each day, discarding all but a small amount before each feeding. It can take a week or two for a new starter to become reliably active, so don't give up too soon. Once it's consistently doubling within 4–8 hours of feeding, it's ready to bake with.

The promise of learning a new language as an adult is not fluency so much as humility. For the first months, you are reduced to the vocabulary of a small child, pointing at things in shops and apologizing for mistakes you can't quite identify. This experience can be frustrating, but it also offers something rare: a daily reminder of how much of our sense of competence depends on context. In a new language, you are forced to rebuild that competence slowly, one word and one conversation at a time — and in doing so, you often discover a different version of yourself.

Starting next month, we're introducing a four-day work week pilot for our entire team. Over the past year, we've seen how focused, well-rested people do their best work, and we want to test whether a shorter week can help us build a healthier and more sustainable culture without compromising the quality of what we deliver for our customers. We'll be sharing what we learn along the way, including the challenges, and we're grateful to our team for their openness and trust as we try something new.

Reminder that you're allowed to change your mind when you learn something new. That's not inconsistency. That's the whole point of learning.

I ran my first marathon last Sunday, and the thing I keep thinking about isn't the finish line. It's the long, quiet training runs in the months before — the early mornings in the cold, the runs where everything hurt and I wanted to stop, the small moments of realizing I could go a little further than the week before. The race itself was wonderful, but the real change happened slowly, in all those ordinary miles nobody saw.

Each lesson takes just five minutes and focuses on the words and phrases you'll actually use — ordering at a café, asking for directions, making small talk with neighbors. Smart review scheduling brings back words right before you're likely to forget them, and short listening exercises help train your ear for real conversations. Whether you're moving abroad or just curious, Wordly helps you build confidence one day at a time.

What does it actually take to build a company that lasts? This week, we sit down with Maya Okafor, founder of the bootstrapped design agency Fieldwork, to talk about growing slowly on purpose. Maya shares why she turned down venture funding, how she thinks about pricing and client relationships, and the hardest lessons from her first five years in business. It's an honest, practical conversation for anyone who wants to build something sustainable on their own terms.

For a slower side of Lisbon, head to the Alfama district early in the morning, before the tour groups arrive. Its narrow, winding streets are best explored without a map — follow the sound of church bells, stop for a pastel de nata at a tiny corner bakery, and climb to one of the miradouros for views across the terracotta rooftops to the river. In the evening, return for dinner at a small tasca, where you may be lucky enough to catch a live fado performance.

Learning to play chess can feel intimidating, especially when you're facing opponents who seem to know dozens of opening names and strategies. The truth is that you don't need to memorize much at all to start enjoying the game. In this guide, we'll cover the basic rules, a few simple principles for the opening, and some common tactics that will help you win more games — along with tips for practicing effectively so you keep improving over time.
